Elon Musk explains why he told SpaceX recruits "we're probably going to die": "With SpaceX, I think there's like a less than 10% chance of being successful, maybe 1%. But if a startup doesn't do something to advance rocket technology, it's definitely not coming from the big defense contractors. So a small chance of success is better than no chance of success." He didn't sell it as a sure thing: "I started that in mid 2002 expecting to fail. Even when recruiting people, I didn't try to make out that it would succeed. I said, we're probably going to die, but there's maybe a 10% chance we might not die, and this is the only way to get people to Mars." That's how he ended up running the engineering himself: "I ended up being chief engineer of the rocket, not because I wanted to, but because I couldn't hire anyone who was good. None of the good chief engineers would join, because they said this is too risky, you're going to die." And the odds were about right: "The first three flights did fail. The fourth one fortunately worked. But if the fourth one hadn't worked, I had no money left, it would have been curtains. We made it by the skin of our teeth." Interested in AI? In February 2004 Elon Musk wrote the check that put Tesla Motors on the road: $6.5 million of a $7.5 million Series A, plus the chairman's seat. He led the next round in February 2005. He co-led the $40 million round in May 2006 that brought in Larry Page and Sergey Brin. That August he published The Secret Tesla Motors Master Plan on the company blog, a sports car to pay for an affordable car, and so on down to the mass market. He pushed for the Roadster's carbon fiber body. By January 2009, Bloomberg reported, he had put $70 million of his own money into the company. CNBC still wrote this on September 10, 2018: "Though Musk didn't found Tesla, his DNA is very much a part of the company." Read the very next sentence of the same article: "He was one of its original investors and chairman of the board in 2004 before becoming CEO in 2008." Original investor. Chairman in 2004. CNBC typed both facts and still filed him under "didn't found." That question had been settled nine years earlier, in court and in writing. In 2009 Martin Eberhard sued, and one of the things he asked a San Mateo County judge for was a declaration that he and Marc Tarpenning were the only two founders. In July the judge struck that request. In September the case was settled and Tesla named five co-founders: Eberhard, Tarpenning, Elon Musk, JB Straubel and Ian Wright. Eberhard's own statement that day: "As a co-founder of the company, Elon's contributions to Tesla have been extraordinary." The man who went to court over the title called Elon Musk a co-founder in his own words. A business network still decided it knew better. Elon Musk has told his side too. In April 2022 he wrote that the Tesla he walked into was "a shell corp" with "literally nothing but a biz plan to commercialize AC Propulsion's Tzero car, which was introduced to me by JB Straubel, *not* Eberhard." Then: "If filing a shell corp constitutes 'founding a company', then I'd be the only founder of PayPal, since I filed the original incorporation docs for http://X.com (later renamed PayPal), but that's not what founding means." And the line that says the most: "I put in all I had, whereas Eberhard, who was worth over $10M at the time, refused to invest a penny to help Tesla." So why slip a false founder line into a 2018 piece? Look at the headline it sat under: "Musk's defiant, rebel CEO persona is putting his company and its investors at risk, say management experts." The article argued Tesla needed "someone to help keep Musk in line." Shrink his role at the birth of the company and it gets much easier to argue he is replaceable at the top of it. Legacy media has been running that play on Elon Musk for years. Tesla closed at $19.03 a share, split-adjusted, the day that story ran. On November 9, 2026 it closed at $378.05. The investors CNBC's experts were so worried about made nearly twenty times their money by keeping him exactly where he was.

Yann LeCun was right the entire time. And generative AI might be a dead end. LeCun has argued that generating every pixel spends too much compute on details instead of learning how the world works. His alternative is JEPA, short for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It predicts what happens next using compressed representations, rather than recreating an image pixel by pixel. One challenge is “representation collapse”: different inputs end up with nearly identical representations, leaving the model with little useful information. Researchers behind LeWorldModel, or LeWM, use a mathematical regularizer to help prevent this. It encourages those representations to follow a Gaussian distribution, simplifying the training setup. LeWM has 15 million parameters and trains on one GPU in a few hours. The researchers report planning up to 48× faster than the foundation world models they compared against. Their experiments also demonstrate physical prediction and detection of impossible events. That does not establish complete understanding of physics or prove generative AI is a dead end. It shows that a small model can learn useful patterns for prediction and planning without generating every pixel.

// Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure // Want to learn how to build agents that speed up LLM training jobs? Check out this paper. InfraRSI raised mean MFU from 17.4% to 30.0% across four dense and MoE training workloads, with speedups up to 2.75x. Why it matters: Coding agents asked to speed up training often produce false speedups. They change the effective batch size, move optimizer steps outside the timing window, or apply unstable low-precision casts. InfraRSI locks a task contract over workload, loss, and timing before any edit. It profiles the baseline and the cluster noise, then searches launch settings and code patches together and re-checks the best candidates against the baseline. It also fits time and peak-memory models across every trial, including out-of-memory failures, and stores what it learns for use on other GPUs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11558 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/infrarsi-harnessing-recursive-self-improvement-for-training-infrastructure-2611.11558

Learn to build a custom harness, folks. This Microsoft work builds a harness to improve long-context reasoning without synthetic data or post-training. (bookmark it) They show that Llama3-8B gains 64.18 points on average across long-context benchmarks with no training at all. The gain comes from the harness. It breaks long-context tasks into capability primitives. A strong agent then rewrites those primitives, the state they track, and the control logic over many rounds of self-improvement on a development set. The harness built for Llama3-8B transfers to Qwen2.5-3B. On HELMET and RULER, it beats NExtLong and PolicyLong, which rely on data synthesis and training, at less than half their estimated cost. The harness is written by GPT-5.6-Sol, and results drop sharply when the small models build their own. The takeaway: before post-training a small model for long context, try improving the harness around it. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10463 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/longcapharness-capability-guided-auto-harnessing-for-long-context-reasoning-2611.10463

Currently working towards a bigger open LLM roundup. But in the meantime, just one of the interesting trends that stood out. I.e., looks like the transition from full to hybrid attention continues. In 2025, there were still lots of full attention models, with a shift to "some full attention" hybrids. In the first half of 2026, the trend towards "some full attention" hybrids continued. And now, in the second half of 2026, we have a 50/50 split between "some full attention" hybrids and models that don't use full attention at all anymore. And yes, there are also no full attention models anymore. The plot legend here means, - Full attention throughout = Global MHA, GQA, dense MLA, CCA in EVERY layer. - Some full attention = Full global attn mixed with: sliding-window/chunked attention, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, Mamba-2, Lightning Attention, convolutions, sparse attention. - No full attention = Zero dense global layers. The main implication is that the trend goes towards making long contexts cheaper to use. This means, it makes the architectures more suitable for long documents and conversations, large code bases, and of course agent usecases that rely on a lot of tool calls. In particular, there are two distinct efficiency gains here: 1) Less attention computation, since sparse attention and the like select tokens or blocks from the context and performs the expensive attention operation from only that subset. (Note that it can still retrieve information from distant positions.) 2) Less memory for retaining context in some architectures, meaning that recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet maintain a fixed-size state. Of course, this saves memory, but compressing the history creates challenges for exact retrieval, so they are usually intermixed with traditional attention methods (sparse or full).

I got this cold email today about what I'd teach kids interested in web development and programming. I figured I'd share my full response here in case it helps others: — Learning to create software today is a glass half full / half empty situation. You can be optimistic or pessimistic. It is strange and transformative that we no longer write most code by hand. AI has completely changed how software is built. I expect this to change even more dramatically in the coming years, as entirely new programming languages¹ are invented² and adopted. One person might look at this and be pessimistic: what will these computer scientists and programmers do, as AI continues to become superhuman in its intelligence? But the wiser of the bunch will realize there is much to be optimistic about. Those with the agency³ to create and explore their wildest ideas have unlimited power. There has quite frankly never been a better time in the history of humanity to have good ideas⁴. So my advice for those building at summer camps is simple. You have to hone and craft your "idea machine". You are going to have lots of bad ideas, but you'll get better at coming up with ideas and refining your taste so you can recognize and act on great ideas sooner. People at summer camps will spend less time reading CS tutorials and more time thinking about the fun or interesting things they want to exist in the world. My favorite way of teaching and getting people interested in software is to first help them build something they are excited about. When they hit roadblocks that require a deeper understanding of a CS concept or something related to web development, only then do we take the time to explain what it is and how it solves their problem. Starting this way, at least for me, seems to get people hooked faster than needing hours and hours of prereqs. There's more desire to spend time learning the fundamentals after having the "aha!" moment. It's worth checking out some skills⁵ designed to help encode the best practices for teaching and then plop that into a coding agent or your AI tool of choice and give it a task: teach me about how databases work (or similar). It's pretty great. It's also worth remembering that AI models today are the worst they will ever be. You need to learn how to be even more ambitious⁶ with what you ask them. Good luck! — ¹ https://x.com/poteto/status/2119824409087348984 ² https://bend-lang.com ³ https://www.neelnanda.io/blog/44-agency ⁴ https://www.are.na/editorial/notes-on-taste ⁵ https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/teach ⁶ https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutorial-for-humans-with-models we are entering a renaissance in programming language and runtime research, and a golden age of software testing and verification it’s time to rewrite all software

Great practical paper on optimizing harness costs. For lower agent costs, you want to change the harness and keep the model. UC Berkeley researchers found that harness changes such as prompts and tools barely move accuracy, but they change cost by up to 2.6x on the same model and task. They analyzed agent traces and found five ways to cut cost. Each one reduces how much context an LLM call reads or how many calls a task needs. Then they built Agency, a layer that sits between existing harnesses like Claude Code and Codex and the model. An optimization written once works across harnesses. Five proof-of-concept techniques cut cost by up to 35% with marginal accuracy loss. If your agent bill keeps growing, look at repeated context reads and extra tool calls before switching models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12122 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/system-optimizations-for-cost-efficient-agent-harnesses-2611.12122

Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth. More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats. Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time. Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices. This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work. Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work. On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary. I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership. https://deepmind.google/blog/formal-verification-signal-protocol

Impressive paper from Robbyant on physical AI. (bookmark it) Robot hands use a range of tactile sensors, and a model trained on one sensor can struggle to transfer to another. That's a big challenge in robotics right now. LingBot-Touch is a foundation model to address this challenge. It was pretrained on 4,983 hours of real touch data. They tested it on the XHand1, a robot hand whose sensor the model never saw. The model stayed frozen. Only a small add-on was trained to find where the fingertip is pressed. On XHand1, the average contact-center error was 0.16 mm with LingBot-Touch versus 5.89 mm with FTP-1 using an XHand1-specific adapter. That's about a 97% reduction in error. It transfers because every sensor maps to the same virtual fingertip. Training also varies touch-point density and placement, so the model can't memorize one sensor. Better touch also makes robots better at tasks. Across six real-world XHand1 tasks, LingBot-VLA averaged 57.21% success both without tactile input and with raw tactile input, rising to 75.04% with LingBot-Touch features. In simulated RL, it scored highest on all twelve tasks. Plate spinning went from 0.5% to 97.4%. Has anyone seen a frozen touch model transfer to a new sensor like this? Paper: http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12806 Code: http://github.com/Robbyant/lingbot-touch Weights: http://huggingface.co/collections/robbyant/lingbot-touch

Great paper from Meta with practical tips for tuning LLM judges. This one is on keeping LLM code judges calibrated and tested on a deployed coding agent. LLM judges often decide whether an agent's code change is good. But their prompts go stale every time the agent changes. AutoRefine fixes the prompt using signals teams already have, like whether tests passed and whether the change got merged.
